chapters.title: History of the Young Man with Spectacles

spans.text: Every story in this book is a lie
Most readers meet The Three Impostors in pieces.
“The Novel of the Black Seal”
and
“The Novel of the White Powder”
have been anthologised for a century, lifted out and printed alone, and they survive the operation well enough that few people notice anything is missing. Something is.

In 1895 Machen did not publish a collection of horror stories. He published a novel in which three criminals hunt a man through London, and in which the horror stories are the tools they hunt him with. Miss Lally, who tells you about Professor Gregg and the black seal, does not exist. Neither does the young man who tells you about the white powder, nor the doctor, nor the grieving sister. They are Helen, Davies and Richmond, wearing names, and every tale they tell is invented on the spot to move a stranger somewhere they want him to be.
This changes what the tales are. Read alone,
“The Novel of the Black Seal”

is a scholar’s account of a discovery that destroyed him. Read in place, it is a performance by a woman who needs Dyson to believe in something, told well enough that it has frightened readers for a hundred and thirty years, and it is not true even inside the book. The impostors are better writers than their victims are readers. That is the joke, and it is a colder one than the horror.

The frame also supplies the only thing the extracted stories lack, which is consequence. The prologue shows you the end before you have seen the beginning: three people leaving a ruined house at night, pleased with themselves, saying farewell to names they will not need again. What they did in that house is withheld until the last pages. Everything between is the long approach to a room the reader has already been shown the outside of.
Lovecraft’s objection, and Machen’s confession
H. P. Lovecraft thought this book contained Machen’s finest work and that the book itself was a mess. In Supernatural Horror in Literature he called it
“a work whose merit as a whole is somewhat marred by an imitation of the jaunty Stevenson manner,”
then spent more words on
“The Novel of the Black Seal”
than on almost anything else he discussed. The verdict has stuck. It is the reason the two famous tales are usually printed without the other twelve sections.
What is less often noticed is that Machen said the same thing first, and said it harder.
In Things Near and Far, his 1923 memoir, he describes setting out in the spring of 1894 to write a book
“which testifies to the vast respect I entertained for the fantastic, ‘New Arabian Nights’ manner of R. L. Stevenson.”
He names the debt without being asked. He goes further:
“The Novel of the Dark Valley,”
the first of the inset tales, is salvage from an earlier book he tore up, and he introduces it as
“to put it mildly, not a very good story.”
He thought the title was bad. He accepted a friend’s judgement that the farce and the tragedy in it were not well mixed. He refused for the rest of his life to write a sequel, because
“the vein was worked out and exhausted: utterly.”

That memoir is printed in full at the back of this edition, and it is the reason to read this book whole rather than in extracts. Lovecraft’s complaint and Machen’s confession are the same complaint. The interesting question is not whether the Stevensonian frame is a flaw, since both of them say it is. The interesting question is why a book its own author dismissed as worked out went on seeding other people’s imaginations for a century.
Where the Little People came from
The answer is mostly in
“The Novel of the Black Seal,”
and it is not a matter of style at all. It is a matter of Machen having taken a piece of respectable Victorian scholarship seriously enough to follow it somewhere no scholar would.
Professor Gregg’s theory, laid out in his own words inside the tale, is that folklore is not invention but garbled memory:
much of the folk-lore of the world is but an exaggerated account of events that really happened.
spans.speaker: Professor Gregg

spans.text: The fairies of Celtic tradition, the Tylwydd Têg, are the surviving rumour of a real people, small, dark, hidden in the hills, displaced by later arrivals and remembered as magic. Gregg pushes it one step further than his sources did and concludes
“that fairies and devils were of one and the same race and origin.”

This was a live idea in the 1880s and 1890s, argued by antiquarians who thought the fairy faith preserved a memory of a pre-Celtic aboriginal population. Machen’s contribution was to ask what would follow if it were true, and to answer without flinching. What follows is a hissing idiot boy, a professor who walks into the hills and does not come back, and a black seal from Babylon whose sixty characters match marks cut into Welsh limestone.
The machinery he built here is worth naming precisely, because it was borrowed wholesale. There is a fragment of a real classical author, Solinus, quoted in real Latin, describing a people who
“hiss rather than speak”

and who venerate a stone called the Hexecontalithos with a secret unspeakable name, Ixaxar. There is the scholar who assembles unrelated evidence into a pattern he would rather not have found. There is the document left behind for others to read. There is a phrase held back until the end and never explained,
“the awful transmutation of the hills,”
which does more work unexplained than any description could.
Anyone who has read the Mythos will recognise all four devices. Machen did them first, and he did them in a book he thought had failed.
1895, and the worst year he could have chosen

The Three Impostors was published by John Lane at the Bodley Head in the Keynotes Series, the most conspicuously modern list in London, the one with the Beardsley title pages. Getting into it should have made him.

It did not, and the memoir explains why in a sentence most readers miss. Heinemann had the manuscript first. They wrote Machen a letter full of praise, read him the reader’s report aloud in their office, quoted the line
“Better than the best of Stevenson,”

pressed an advance on royalties on him, and hoped their house might publish his beautiful books for ever. Three weeks later the manuscript came back with a printed rejection slip. He describes himself afterwards as a pantomime policeman on a buttered slide,
rolling in the mud, sprawling, my legs in the air.
Then the year itself went wrong. The Wilde trials ran through the spring and summer of 1895 and made anything decadent commercially poisonous. Machen’s own account is dry about it: there had been
“some ugly scandals in the summer of ‘95, which had made people impatient with reading matter that was not obviously and obtrusively ‘healthy’.”
A book of London decadence, published by the Bodley Head, in the Beardsley series, in that autumn, was as badly timed as a book can be. The reviewers, he recalled, took the view that he was
“something of a pretentious ass”
and that his horrors
“were all humbug.”
What survived

The book failed on its own terms and Machen never argued otherwise. What survived is stranger than a success would have been. Two inset tales escaped the frame and entered the permanent stock of weird fiction. A theory about fairies became a theory about gods. A phrase about the hills, left undefined on purpose, turned out to be the most influential sentence he ever wrote.

This edition prints all fourteen sections in their original order, because the tales were built to be told by liars and read that way they are better, not worse. The headnotes mark where each inset tale begins, who is supposed to be telling it, and what that person actually wants. The glossary covers the Latin, the Welsh and the London that Machen expected his readers to know and no longer can. And Machen’s own account of writing the thing, of the Heinemann letter and the bad year and the reviews, is printed at the back so that the last word on the book belongs to him.

Machen shows you the ending first. Three people leave a decaying house at night, pleased with themselves, and say goodbye to the names they have been using: Mr. Burton the dealer in curiosities, Mr. Wilkins the private secretary, Miss Lally and Miss Leicester. Those four names belong to narrators you are about to meet and believe. Watch what the girl is carrying in the paper parcel, and what she says it came from. The scene is never explained here. Everything in the book after this point happens before it.
And Mr. Joseph Walters is going to stay the night?
said the smooth clean-shaven man to his companion, an individual not of the most charming appearance, who had chosen to make his ginger-colored mustache merge into a pair of short chin-whiskers.

The two stood at the hall door, grinning evilly at each other; and presently a girl ran quickly down the stairs, and joined them. She was quite young, with a quaint and piquant rather than a beautiful face, and her eyes were of a shining hazel. She held a neat paper parcel in one hand, and laughed with her friends.
Leave the door open,
said the smooth man to the other, as they were going out.
Yes, by----,
he went on with an ugly oath.
We'll leave the front door on the jar. He may like to see company, you know.
The other man looked doubtfully about him.
Is it quite prudent do you think, Davies?
he said, pausing with his hand on the mouldering knocker.
I don't think Lipsius would like it. What do you say, Helen?

I agree with Davies. Davies is an artist, and you are commonplace, Richmond, and a bit of a coward. Let the door stand open, of course. But what a pity Lipsius had to go away! He would have enjoyed himself.
Yes,
replied the smooth Mr. Davies,
that summons to the west was very hard on the doctor.
The three passed out, leaving the hall door, cracked and riven with frost and wet, half open, and they stood silent for a moment under the ruinous shelter of the porch.
Well,
said the girl,
it is done at last. I shall hurry no more on the track of the young man with spectacles.
We owe a great deal to you,
spans.speaker: Davies

spans.text: said Mr. Davies politely;

"the doctor said so before he left. But have we not all three some farewells to make? I, for my part, propose to say good-by, here, before this picturesque but mouldy residence, to my friend Mr. Burton, dealer in the antique and curious,"
and the man lifted his hat with an exaggerated bow.
And I,
spans.speaker: Richmond

spans.text: said Richmond,
bid adieu to Mr. Wilkins, the private secretary, whose company has, I confess, become a little tedious.
spans.speaker: Richmond

spans.text: Farewell to Miss Lally, and to Miss Leicester also,
said the girl, making as she spoke a delicious courtesy.
Farewell to all occult adventure; the farce is played.
Mr. Davies and the lady seemed full of grim enjoyment, but Richmond tugged at his whiskers nervously.
I feel a bit shaken up,
he said.
I've seen rougher things in the States, but that crying noise he made gave me a sickish feeling. And then the smell--But my stomach was never very strong.

The three friends moved away from the door, and began to walk slowly up and down what had been a gravel path, but now lay green and pulpy with damp mosses. It was a fine autumn evening, and a faint sunlight shone on the yellow walls of the old deserted house, and showed the patches of gangrenous decay, and all the stains, the black drift of rain from the broken pipes, the scabrous blots where the bare bricks were exposed, the green weeping of a gaunt laburnum that stood beside the porch, and ragged marks near the ground where the reeking clay was gaining on the worn foundations. It was a queer rambling old place, the centre perhaps two hundred years old, with dormer windows sloping from the tiled roof, and on each side there were Georgian wings; bow windows had been carried up to the first floor, and two dome-like cupolas that had once been painted a bright green were now gray and neutral. Broken urns lay upon the path, and a heavy mist seemed to rise from the unctuous clay; the neglected shrubberies, grown all tangled and unshapen, smelt dank and evil, and there was an atmosphere all about the deserted mansion that proposed thoughts of an opened grave. The three friends looked dismally at the rough grasses and the nettles that grew thick over lawn and flower-beds; and at the sad water-pool in the midst of the weeds. There, above green and oily scum instead of lilies, stood a rusting Triton on the rocks, sounding a dirge through a shattered horn; and beyond, beyond the sunk fence and the far meadows, the sun slid down and shone red through the bars of the elm trees.
Richmond shivered and stamped his foot.
We had better be going soon,
spans.speaker: Richmond

spans.text: he said;
there is nothing else to be done here.
spans.speaker: Richmond

spans.text: No,
spans.speaker: Davies

spans.text: said Davies,

it is finished at last. I thought for some time we should never get hold of the gentleman with the spectacles. He was a clever fellow, but, Lord! he broke up badly at last. I can tell you he looked white at me when I touched him on the arm in the bar. But where could he have hidden the thing? We can all swear it was not on him.
spans.speaker: Davies

spans.text: The girl laughed, and they turned away, when Richmond gave a violent start.
Ah!
spans.speaker: Richmond

spans.text: he cried, turning to the girl,
what have you got there? Look, Davies, look! it's all oozing and dripping.
spans.speaker: Richmond

spans.text: The young woman glanced down at the little parcel she was carrying, and partially unfolded the paper.
Yes, look both of you,
she said;
it's my own idea. Don't you think it will do nicely for the doctor's museum? It comes from the right hand, the hand that took the gold Tiberius.
Mr. Davies nodded with a good deal of approbation, and Richmond lifted his ugly high-crowned bowler, and wiped his forehead with a dingy handkerchief.
I'm going,
he said;
you two can stay if you like.

The three went round by the stable path, past the withered wilderness of the old kitchen garden, and struck off by a hedge at the back, making for a particular point in the road. About five minutes later two gentlemen, whom idleness had led to explore these forgotten outskirts of London, came sauntering up the shadowy carriage drive. They had spied the deserted house from the road, and as they observed all the heavy desolation of the place they began to moralize in the great style, with considerable debts to Jeremy Taylor.
Look, Dyson,
said the one as they drew nearer,
look at those upper windows; the sun is setting, and though the panes are dusty, yet
The grimy sash an oriel burns.
Phillipps,
replied the elder and (it must be said) the more pompous of the two,

I yield to fantasy, I cannot withstand the influence of the grotesque. Here, where all is falling into dimness and dissolution, and we walk in cedarn gloom, and the very air of heaven goes mouldering to the lungs, I cannot remain commonplace. I look at that deep glow on the panes, and the house lies all enchanted; that very room, I tell you, is within all blood and fire.
